body: Thanks for the explanation and suggestion! I've implemented it in the PR 😄

This should use a zigzag line, like other IDEs and text editors. A flat line doesn't really convey warning as well.
It could use multiple line segments or an svg per character that makes a repeating pattern, or calculate the points for the entire line and use `draw_polyline`.

This can be a LocalVector since it isn't being passed around.

Also can be moved to right after the struct.
The color should be configurable, and to make sure it works on all color schemes. (See `EditorThemeManager::_populate_text_editor_styles`).
Is there a reason this is only for warnings and not errors?

Also the underline should update on text change, since parsing can be slow and would cause it to become out of sync. Especially when adding or removing lines above it. 
Probably in `TextEdit::_text_changed`, and I imagine it would be a function similar to `TextEdit::_offset_carets_after` but for underlines.
Unused?
Looks like it is indeed - I think it was a remnant of a previous approach I'd tried to determining which characters were encompassed by the underline range 😅 Will remove it for now

As of right now, the reason is pretty much just that I wanted to get the idea down and logic working with warnings before trying to replicate it for errors. I don't expect it should be difficult to add error support, so maybe I'll try doing that later today.

I agree, a zigzag line would fit much better with conventions. The main reason I avoided it for this initial version was that I wasn't sure how I'd get it to seamlessly loop across characters.

Perhaps with a monospace font, we can assume all the characters will have equal width and thus design a single line segment to be the width of a single character, so that when they're repeatedly drawn next to each other they look like a seamless looping zigzag. I feel like I might remember seeing people use non-monospace fonts in the code editor, though, which would break this approach if so?

Determining the per-line spans of underlined characters, and then drawing a single polyline that follows that range, would probably be the best solution but would require a bit more work. I'll try to give that a shoot soon though!

```suggestion
	void _offset_underlines_after(int p_old_line, int p_old_column, int p_new_line, int p_new_column);

```
I'd keep this for readability

If the warning line is set to transparent it would prevent the underline from working.
So this condition can be changed to check if both don't have an alpha of zero, and new checks can be added inside the loop for the colors individually.
Same with error below.
The underline colors can probably be considered basic settings, they can be added here.
Underlines should be swapped too for `swap_lines()`.

There should be a check to prevent `canvas_item_add_polyline` from drawing if there are less than 2 points, it looks like it could happen if `TS->shaped_text_get_selection` returns a zero distance for any reason. (There are zero width characters, or the start and end positions could be the same).

> I noticed that in the first video, when typing before the unknown variable this_does_not_exist, the newly typed text doesn't get underlined until it re-parses (expected behavior); however, typing after the variable results in the newly typed text instantly being underlined. I suppose this still ends up being valid? But if I can figure out how to resolve that later, that might be nice for consistency's sake.

This was controlled by the `bool p_include_selection_begin = true, bool p_include_selection_end = true` parameters. Having both as true makes sure that removing text changes the selection appropriately, but it causes inserting text at the end to expand the range. For example `insert_text` has `bool p_before_selection_begin = true, bool p_before_selection_end = false`, which are in effect the same parameters but renamed for inserting, and the different defaults are better for inserting text.

`p_include_selection_begin` doubles as an option to insert before or after the caret when there is no selection, but that's not really applicable to underlines. Sometimes when the selection starts or ends at the beginning of a line different insert functions have different behavior when inserting new lines to expand the selection or not.
But I don't think we care about that for underlines, we probably don't ever want an underline to grow when text is added at the edges.

So we could either add a parameter or detect when text is inserted vs removed to determine whether to include the underline end, which should just be `bool include_end = edit_height == 0 ? edit_size < 0 : edit_height < 0;`
Underline thickness and height should probably scale with font size.
Are these intentionally ints instead of floats? It loses precision.

The distance between points should probably be related to the width of a single character, rather than hardcoded, so it will better scale to different sizes. Like `char_w / 2` or something.
(And the font is probably monospace, but even if its not we don't need to worry even if the actual character here is a different size.)

Sometimes the underline will go past the last char: It would be better if it clamped to the point, even if it is not at the top or bottom position. Here is some pseudocode to get the vertical position of the last point. The y portion should be the same as the x portion since it is linear. ```cpp float last_point_portion = (end_position - points[points.size() - 1].x) / distance; float last_point_y = squiggle_top_y + combined_rect.size.y * (current_squiggle_side == squiggle_top_y ? last_point_portion : 1.0 - last_point_portion) ``` And there may need to be a check to make sure it is not too close to the last position, especially if the end point does already match the end of the character perfectly.
Should use `text_ci` instead of `ci`.
Did the `include_end` approach have issues? Doing `ul_end_line == p_new_line && ul_end_column > p_new_column` doesn't cover all cases.

There is a clipping issue here (even when using text_ci) the warnings show over the gutter/minimap when scrolling horizontally. They should be cut off when out of bounds. Or it could wait for a PR that separates the text CI from gutters and minimap (like I'm working on in https://github.com/kitbdev/godot/tree/text-edit-h-text-clip) A check like this should fix it: ```cpp if (distance >= xmargin_beg && distance <= xmargin_end) { ```

This would be more efficient if it just checked all lines in all underlines, instead of all underlines on all lines.
Ideally it would only separate the underlines on the affected lines too, but I guess it doesn't really matter like you said.

For an example of where this code is called use the Convert Indentation to spaces/tabs options, the intent with the carets is to keep them at the same visual place it was, even though the exact column has changed.
But I don't think we care enough to have to do that with underlines, so it should be fine.

I thought I remembered drawing operations themselves only working with ints. I must've mixed Godot's APIs up with something else's 😅
Will use floats instead!

Thanks, I've incorporated `char_w / 2.0` instead of a hardcoded value and for the most part I think it looks better! With the current way the path is calculated, the underline for a single character looks a little unusual: Looking at VS Code, I think they might use a similar strategy (squiggle pattern is per character) but they use some kind of sine wave instead: So I might see if I can rework the point calculation to do something more like VS Code, that more clearly reads as an underline squiggle instead of some kind of caret.
Using the solution you proposed up above of making a single squiggle pattern as wide as the character it covers also fixes this problem, as far as I can tell:

Thanks, that check is working well!

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/fb69eca3-842e-4055-a696-e88f273c5e7d

Looks like there may be a very slight visual issue where an underline can't be partially off-screen, but the same applies to the characters themselves, so I imagine that'd have to be covered by something like your PR. Until then, I think this looks good 🙂
Underline thickness now scales with font size (and base scale); I will do the same for the squiggle height when I write a new algorithm for doing the sine-style squiggles!

It looks like VSCode uses an svg with 3 overlapping polygons, so when scaled to a character, it looks more rounded than it actually is: It's basically a straight zigzag with the corners cut off. I don't know if we need to do that, but I do think it is a good idea to make it less like a caret symbol when small by making it start in the middle and go up and down. It should be possible to offset the pattern by half of the distance between points and manually set the start and end points.

Neat, thanks for looking into VS Code's implementation!

I was thinking of using a similar approach to what I'm doing currently (drawing a polyline with calculated points) but following a similar shape to VS Code:
- First point at (0, 0)
- Second point at (0.25, 1)
- Third point at (0.75, -1)
- Fourth point at (1, 0) - maybe omit this if it's not the last underline to be drawn, so we're not putting down duplicate vertices for the end point of underline i and the start point of underline i + 1

Then, the coordinates would be scaled to match the space underneath each character:
- x = 0 is left edge of character, x = 1 is right edge
- y = 0 is a distance underneath the character, y = 1 is underneath the character but closer to the bottom edge, y = -1 is farther from the bottom edge

Do you foresee issues with an approach like this, in contrast to keeping the current zigzag-drawing behavior but offsetting it?

I don't think it should be scaled to each character individually, I imagine it would look weird to change frequency with each character that is a different size, especially on tabs. Note VSCode doesn't scale it per character, it repeats the pattern until it fills the entire width, and then somehow cuts it off. Sorry, I meant when the svg was sampled at the resolution appropriate for the font size that it looks rounder than it actually is, not that it is actually scaled for each character width. Using a fixed value (the current `distance_between_points`) as the 0.5 distance between points 2 and 3 as they repeat would be better. Here is some non-uniform text if you want it ```gdscript func _test_lang(): var variable := "test string" var عامل := "سلسلة الاختبار" var מִשְׁתַנֶה := "מחרוזת בדיקה" var 变量 := "测试 字符串" var 変数 := "テスト 文字列" # テスト　文学 var 변수 := "테스트 문자열" var emoji := "👏👏👏👏👏" ```
`base_scale` can be used for thickness, but I'm not sure about using it for the squiggle height, I think only the font size would matter for it. Probably.

Makes sense! In my attempt with this new approach I used `char_w` as the character width and realized when checking its definition that it should be a consistent width no matter the specific character being covered, so I think it all works out! I'm now getting squiggles that look pretty good even with different sized characters like tabs 🙂

Thanks for letting me know about the Convert Indentation options. I just tested them and there is a momentary weird offset on the underlines due to the columns changing, before Godot re-evaluates the script and updates the underlines:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d7df9703-daa1-40d9-b7ab-6f5c6089f079

It's a bit ugly so I think I may do some investigating and see if it can be fixed. But if it seems like it's turning into a big rabbit-hole, given the fact that it resolves itself fairly quickly (and, looking at the calls to `set_text()` in the codebase, it shouldn't be something called _that_ often) I'm not sure if it would be worth spending too much time on or blocking the rest of the PR from moving forward.

It may be easier to instead change the Convert Indentation to spaces/tabs options to use `remove_text` and `insert_text` and avoid the use of `set_line`.
It would mean if the caret was on the indentation it would get moved to the end, but its not really a big deal.

With the non-uniform text example you provided, I see the squiggle frequency remains consistent, but depending on individual character width it can end up going past the end of a character a bit: Later, I'll take another look at the algorithm and the pseudocode you provided for cutting off the squiggle immediately at the end of the character.
Squiggles now cut off mid-segment!

That does sound a lot more efficient! I have some ideas on how to implement this algorithm more efficiently along with iterating over the underlines primarily, and should be able to get to that tomorrow or early this upcoming week.

It took a little while, but I've implemented an algorithm that I think should be more efficient! It iterates over each underline, and only replaces/splits it if it touches one of the lines to be swapped. The original underline data for the swapped lines is then "pasted" in to their new positions.

It was admittedly a bit confusing to me originally when I tried to implement it, and it seemed like the other approach I tried was working for my test case.

I went back to it tonight and think I got a better grasp on what it's doing. It seems to be working here:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/68582b5a-abfb-4b59-8a83-ddd470403889

Undoing still seems to leave the underlines in an invalid state for a brief moment before the script is re-evaluated. I see from a quick `print_line` test that undoing doesn't actually call `_offset_underlines_after`, so in order to fix that I'd have to look into how the TextEdit handles undos/redos.

Do you think it would be necessary to fix this visual bug, or could it be left alone for now (perhaps addressed in the future if it causes more problems or is found by users to be annoying)?

Note that VS Code _does_ reposition underlines properly as part of an undo operation:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/472938d2-a3f0-496c-80de-8b80c389e13d

Undo/redo saves caret positions, so it doesn't call `_offset_carets_after`, see `TextEdit::_do_text_op`. It should be possible to add `_offset_underlines_after` there, but its going to lose information either way and won't always get back to its original state, so I think its fine to leave it for now.
This should be fine, I don't think we need to respect the selection parameters for underlines.
We should probably turn on antialiasing for this by passing true.

Couldn't this last one be deleted? Changing it to be 3 vertices won't change things since it just iterates through them and this is the same as the first one. It's only adding adding duplicate points.

And the first one could also be removed to just be a special case when its the first point, it doesn't need to be added to points again. Because the code to cut off at the end position will run anyway.
This assumes that text is added/removed at the start of the line which isn't always the case for other uses of set_line. But it probably doesn't matter.

Thanks, yep looks like it! I was able to simplify it down such that it doesn't even need the custom struct (just alternates between top and bottom using a bool). I suppose in the future if we wanted to do a more complex squiggle pattern, the struct approach could come in handy again, but we could also probably just write a math function that computes the points given a distance across. For now, though, I think this works well 🙂

The underline colors are not in the highlighting section, which means they won't be saved as a part of the text editor color theme. This probably isn't what we want, so it should be moved into `text_editor/theme/highlighting/`.

This would also fix the issue where you can't change the underline color when on a non-custom color preset. (since it immediately overwrites it instead of being updated to Custom)

The colors are updated here, but any existing underlines are not updated until they are re-parsed.
Above, it updates the bg colors like `text_edit->set_line_background_color(i, updated_warning_line_color);`, but underlines need to do similar.

Done! Now when the colors are updated, it goes through the underlines and updates any underlines with a color that matches the _current_ color for the given type (warning or error), similar to how the line backgrounds work above.

While writing out this explanation, it did occur to me that there might be potential for a bug, including in the already-existing line background code: if two background or underline types have the same color, and then one of the colors is changed, then the editor may update both to the new color, instead of just the type that was actually changed. If this is indeed the case, I imagine the editor re-evaluates the script and corrects the mistake pretty quickly, so it only ends up being a visual bother for a few moments. But it could be a good thing to investigate fixing in another PR.

Can we maybe just keep the old structure for `ScritpLanguageExtension` for the time being? I want to move those API's somewhere else, and IMO it would make more sense to keep the old format here, and exclusively support the new one in the new API.

By "keep the old structure" do you mean keep `line` and `column` keys but with the meaning of the new `start_line` and `start_column` keys, then add `end_line` and `end_column` as well? The information about the end of the error range needs to be passed through this method in order to make it to the language server/script editor, as far as I know.

I mean only accept `line` and `column` from this API.

The only actual usage of this API that I was able to locate on public Github is https://github.com/maiself/godot-python-extension which is a work-in-progress project.

We are adding those new features for internal use, it is IMO too early to expose them, when there is no one asking for it right now.

To my understanding, doing that would mean the error underlines would be less precise, and always span an entire line instead of just the portion actually causing the error. If that is okay for the PR, I can make the change soon.
IMHO `ScriptLanguageExtension` at the moment should be focused on compatibility, so this should be fine, since that's how it is right now anyway.

Yeah that's exactly what I meant. Changing the internal structs is totally fine. I just don't want to expose it for now, because I want to move `validate` into `EditorLanguage` soonish. And exposing this now, would make the compat code more complicated. Sorry for the confusion :sweat:
No worries! In retrospect the description/request you gave made perfect sense and I just did a bad job of interpreting it initially. So apologies from my end 😅

Indeed. That's the major caveat when comments are involved. They tend to become outdated, so beware of that.
Makes sense! I think it can be shortened down to "Ensure the underline ends at the end of the text" and convey essentially the same information, so I'll do that to keep it from being verbose.
